summary: This RFC defines TLVs for carrying cryptographic integrity check values, such as signatures or message authentication codes, and timestamps in the generalized MANET packet and message format of RFC 5444. It was replaced by RFC 7182.

plainLanguage.summary: A message can carry a sealed stamp proving it was not changed, plus a clock reading. This defined where to put those on wireless mesh messages.

subtitle: A standard way to attach cryptographic signatures and timestamps to wireless mesh network control messages.

tldr.problem: Mobile ad hoc networks (MANETs) use routing protocols that exchange control messages to discover neighbors and routes. These messages can be forged or modified by attackers. Protocols needed a standard way to include cryptographic integrity check values (ICVs) and timestamps without building security into every protocol.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 6622 defines Type-Length-Value (TLV) fields that can be attached to MANET packets, messages, and addresses to carry ICVs (computed as a cryptographic function over a hash) and timestamps. It also establishes registries for hash functions and cryptographic functions.
tldr.outcome: The specification was replaced by RFC 7182. The TLV framework allows MANET routing protocols to verify message authenticity without reimplementing security mechanisms for each protocol.

facts.label: Supported hash functions
facts.value: None (identity), SHA-1, SHA-224, SHA-256, SHA-384, SHA-512

facts.label: Supported crypto functions
facts.value: None, RSA, DSA, HMAC, 3DES, AES, ECDSA

today: RFC 6622 is a Proposed Standard in the Internet Standards Track and has been superseded by RFC 7182. The TLV framework allows MANET routing protocols and extensions to add authentication and freshness information without reimplementing security mechanisms for each protocol.

sections.title: MANET Security Through TLVs
sections.content:
Mobile Ad Hoc Networks (MANETs) are wireless networks without fixed infrastructure where nodes communicate by forwarding messages through multiple hops. MANET routing protocols exchange control messages to discover neighbors and compute routes. Attackers can forge or modify these messages, disrupting the network.

Rather than building security into each routing protocol, RFC 5444 defined a generalized packet and message format with extensible Type-Length-Value (TLV) fields. RFC 6622 uses this framework to define how to carry cryptographic integrity check values (ICVs) and timestamps in TLVs. This allows any MANET routing protocol to add security without reimplementation.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of each network protocol having its own way to seal messages, there is a standard way to stick a seal on the message. Any protocol can use it.

sections.title: The TLV Framework
sections.content:
RFC 6622 defines six TLV types: two for packets (ICV and Timestamp), two for messages (ICV and Timestamp), and two for address blocks (ICV and Timestamp). Each TLV type can carry different kinds of data through type extensions. For example, an ICV TLV with type extension 0 contains raw integrity check value bytes with no predefined structure. Type extension 1 specifies that the ICV is computed as a cryptographic function applied to a hash value, with fields indicating which hash function and cryptographic function are used.

The RFC also establishes IANA registries for hash functions (SHA-1, SHA-256, SHA-384, SHA-512) and cryptographic functions (RSA, DSA, HMAC, 3DES, AES, ECDSA) that can be used when computing ICVs.
sections.plainLanguage: The TLV is like a slot machine: you can put different kinds of coins (data) in the same slot, and the machine knows what to do with each type.

sections.title: Signing Packets and Messages
sections.content:
A Packet ICV TLV contains the integrity check value of an entire packet. The ICV is calculated over the whole packet, including the packet header and all contained messages, but excluding any Packet ICV TLVs already present. Before calculating the ICV, existing ICV TLVs are removed and then restored afterward, allowing multiple ICVs with different algorithms to be added to the same packet.

A Message ICV TLV contains the integrity check value of a single message. When calculating the ICV, the hop limit and hop count fields are both assumed to be zero, because these fields are mutable (they change as the message is forwarded). This allows any node to verify the ICV even after the message has been forwarded multiple times.
sections.plainLanguage: The seal covers the whole message as it was when sent. When a message travels through many nodes, the nodes change some parts of it (like the hop counter), but the seal was calculated ignoring those parts so the seal still works.

sections.title: Signing Individual Addresses
sections.content:
An Address Block ICV TLV is associated with an address or a set of addresses and protects the integrity of that address plus any other attributes carried with it in other TLVs. The ICV is calculated over the address and any concatenated attribute values from other TLV types associated with the address.

If both a Timestamp TLV and an ICV TLV are associated with an address, the timestamp value is included in the ICV calculation. This ties the timestamp to the ICV, preventing attackers from modifying the timestamp without invalidating the integrity check.
sections.plainLanguage: Each address in a message can have its own seal. If an address also has a time stamp, the seal covers the timestamp too.

sections.title: How to Calculate ICVs
sections.content:
When type extension 1 is used, the ICV is computed as a cryptographic function applied to a hash value of the content. The ICV TLV value contains four parts: a hash function indicator (one byte specifying SHA-256, SHA-1, etc.), a cryptographic function indicator (one byte specifying RSA, DSA, HMAC, etc.), a key identifier length (one byte), and optionally a key identifier, followed by the ICV result.

The key identifier allows a receiver to select the correct key from a key store. A key identifier length of zero means a pre-installed shared key is used. The length of the ICV result is computed length minus 3 minus key-identifier-length, allowing ICVs of varying sizes depending on the cryptographic function chosen.
sections.plainLanguage: To make the seal, you hash the message, then encrypt the hash with your private key. The seal shows which hash method and which encryption method were used, and which key was used.

sections.title: Timestamps for Freshness
sections.content:
Timestamp TLVs carry freshness information about when an ICV was calculated. Each TLV type (Packet, Message, or Address Block Timestamp) can have different type extensions representing different timestamp formats: arbitrary-length unsigned integers, 32-bit POSIX timestamps, NTP timestamps, or signed arbitrary-length integers.

How timestamps are interpreted is left to the MANET routing protocol using this specification. They could represent seconds since the UNIX epoch, GPS time, or a simple incrementing sequence number. The important part is that the standard defines where the timestamp is placed and how it is included in ICV calculations.
sections.plainLanguage: The timestamp is like a date on a letter. The routing protocol decides whether the date means seconds, or microseconds, or just a count of messages.
